Migrating to apaTables 4.0

Source: vignettes/migrating-to-4.0.Rmd
migrating-to-4.0.Rmd

Who this guide is for

This guide is for code written for apaTables 2.0.8, the version on CRAN before 4.0.0. It lists what you may need to change and what now behaves differently. (Versions 3.0.0 and 3.0.1 were never released to CRAN. If you installed one of them from GitHub, the last section is for you.)

What keeps working

The table functions – apa.cor.table(), apa.reg.table(), apa.d.table(), apa.aov.table(), apa.1way.table() and apa.2way.table() – keep the same names and every argument from 2.0.8, so most scripts that build tables with them run unchanged. What changes is the kind of file they write, some default settings, some names inside the table object, and some of the numbers in ANOVA and hierarchical regression tables, where 2.0.8 had errors. A few scripts now stop with a message instead – a file name with an unusual ending, regression blocks that do not build on one another, a model with an offset, or a setting outside the values a function accepts. Each is described below.

Two functions were removed

apa.ezANOVA.table() is gone, because the ez package it relied on was archived on CRAN. Use apa.afex.table() instead, with the output of afex::aov_ez(). It covers between-participant, repeated-measures and mixed designs. The afex package does not come with apaTables; install it once with install.packages("afex").

goggles_results <- afex::aov_ez(id = "participant",
     dv = "attractiveness", data = goggles,
     between = c("gender", "alcohol"))
apa.afex.table(afex.output = goggles_results)

apa.reg.boot.table() is gone too, and there is no replacement in this release: apaTables 4.0 does not make bootstrapped regression tables. apa.reg.table() still makes the standard regression table.

Files are now Word .docx files

In 2.0.8, filename = "Table1.doc" wrote an RTF file with a .doc name. The same code in 4.0 writes a real Word file named Table1.docx, and prints a message naming the file each time:

my_table <- apa.cor.table(data = attitude, filename = "Table1.doc")
# apaTables 4.0 writes Word files in .docx format (the legacy .doc/.rtf
# RTF engine was retired). Writing: Table1.docx

A .rtf name is handled the same way. Change the name to .docx and the message stops. A name ending in .html writes a web page instead. A name ending in .pdf stops with a message explaining how to make a PDF table (see “Tables in Quarto documents” below), and any other ending, or none, stops with an error asking for .docx or .html (2.0.8 wrote a file under any name).

apa.save() is new in 4.0, and it is the usual way to write tables to a file. Build the table on one line and save it on the next:

my_table <- apa.cor.table(data = attitude)
apa.save(filename = "Table1.docx", my_table)

It also writes several tables to a single Word file, one table per page:

table1 <- apa.cor.table(data = attitude)
table2 <- apa.reg.table(lm(rating ~ complaints + privileges, data = attitude))
apa.save(filename = "Tables.docx", table1, table2)

The pages are US letter. Add paper = "a4" for A4.

Tables are numbered 1 unless you say otherwise

In 2.0.8, table.number defaulted to NA: a table built without one had no number at the console, and the file said “Table XX”. It now defaults to 1. A number you supply is used as before. To leave a table unnumbered, use table.number = 0 (or NA, or NULL).

When apa.save() writes several tables to one file, a number you supplied is kept, and a table left at the default takes the next number after the last numbered table before it, starting at 1. Three tables left at the default become Table 1, Table 2 and Table 3. If the second is given table.number = 5, they become Table 1, Table 5 and Table 6.

Which tables are printed sideways

In 2.0.8 the orientation of each file was fixed by the function that wrote it:

  • apa.cor.table(), apa.d.table() and apa.2way.table() wrote a landscape (sideways) page unless you passed landscape = FALSE;
  • apa.reg.table() always wrote a landscape page;
  • apa.1way.table() wrote an upright page unless you passed landscape = TRUE;
  • apa.aov.table() always wrote an upright page.

In 4.0 every table function takes a landscape argument (apa.reg.table() and apa.aov.table() gain it), and by default apaTables measures the table and turns the page only when the table does not fit upright. In the Word files that apa.save() (or filename =) writes:

  • small d-value and two-way tables, such as the examples on the help pages, and correlation tables of up to about five variables, now print upright; larger ones still turn sideways when they need to;
  • regression tables are wide enough that they usually still print sideways.

landscape = TRUE gives you a landscape page whether the table needs it or not. landscape = FALSE keeps the page upright; a table too wide for it is set in smaller type so that every column is kept.

In a Quarto manuscript, apaTables measures each table against the page and type size of the manuscript, so more tables stay upright there – a one-block regression table, for example.

Numbers that can differ from 2.0.8

These changes correct errors in 2.0.8, so a table can show different numbers from the one 2.0.8 printed for the same model:

  • apa.aov.table(), Type III (the default). If your model was fitted with the R default contrasts and had an interaction, 2.0.8 printed each main effect at one level of the other factor rather than the main effect. In the goggles example, alcohol printed as F = 0.61, p = .546 instead of F = 20.07, p < .001. apaTables 4.0 refits the model with sum-to-zero contrasts, as SPSS does, so the table is right whether or not you set options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", "contr.poly")). If you already set that line, your main effects are unchanged.
  • apa.aov.table(), all types. 2.0.8 rounded the sums of squares and F to two decimals before computing the mean squares, partial eta-squared and the confidence interval for it, so those could be off by .01, or print as NaN for a dependent variable on a very small scale. They are now computed at full precision and rounded only when printed. With type = 2, the confidence interval for the first effect is no longer blank.
  • apa.reg.table() with several blocks. 2.0.8 accepted blocks that did not build on one another and printed a negative change in R2 with a [NaN, NaN] interval. Each block must now contain every predictor of the block before it, plus at least one more, and all blocks must be fitted to the same cases. Code that broke these rules now stops with a message saying what to change.
  • apa.reg.table() intervals for the semi-partial correlation squared and the change in R2. 2.0.8 could print a negative lower limit for these proportions of variance. The limits are now held to the range 0 to 1, so such a limit prints as .00.
  • apa.d.table(). 2.0.8 left a d-value and the interval for it blank (- and [-,-]) when Levene’s test, centered on the median, gave p < .05 for that pair of groups. A d-value is now reported for every pair, computed with the pooled standard deviation as before, and no test of equal variances is run. Compare the standard deviations in the table to judge whether one pooled value describes both groups.
  • Significance stars. A p value of exactly .01 was unmarked in 2.0.8; it is now marked with one star.
  • apa.2way.table() marginal means. 2.0.8 counted a case with a missing value on one factor in the marginal mean of the other factor, though it was in no cell. Marginal means now use only the cases in the cells.

Settings that now stop with a message

apaTables 4.0 checks these settings, and a value it does not accept stops with a message naming the values allowed:

  • conf.level in apa.aov.table() and prop.var.conf.level in apa.reg.table() must be .90 or .95 (2.0.8 silently used .90 and .95, respectively, in place of any other value);
  • landscape must be TRUE, FALSE or NA;
  • table.number must be a whole number, 0 or more.

apa.reg.table() and apa.aov.table() also stop for a model with an offset (an offset() term, or the offset argument of lm()). In 2.0.8, apa.reg.table() printed the offset as a predictor row with no estimate. Fit the model without the offset.

New p values and n columns

A correlation table now prints the p value for each correlation on a line below the confidence interval. To leave those lines out, as 2.0.8 did, add show.pvalue = FALSE:

my_table <- apa.cor.table(data = attitude, show.pvalue = FALSE)

Correlation tables also gain an N column, the number of cases for each variable. When the data have missing values, the note gives the range of the number of cases behind each correlation. d-value and one-way tables gain an n column, the number of cases in each group.

If your script reads values out of the table object

Most scripts only print or save a table. If yours reads values out of the object a table function returns, these changed:

  • Correlation, d-value, one-way and two-way tables now use the same names as regression and ANOVA tables already did: table_number, table_title, table_body and table_note instead of table.number, table.title, table.body and table.note. The old names now give NULL. The object class is apa_table (it was apa.table for those four).
  • In a regression table, the columns sr2 and sr2_95%_CI are now Unique_R2 and Unique_95%_CI (the interval column follows prop.var.conf.level, so Unique_90%_CI at .90), and the Unique_R2 values carry significance stars, so as.numeric() on that column no longer works. In a table with several blocks, the Difference column is now Delta_Fit, and each block starts with a “Model 1”, “Model 2”, … row, so the predictor rows sit one row lower per block.
  • In an ANOVA table, a very small p value prints as <.001 rather than .000.
  • A correlation table has the new N column and the p value lines.
  • d-value and one-way tables have a new n column, the number of cases in each group, after the variable names.
  • Titles and notes are worded differently, in APA title case. For example, “Means, standard deviations, and correlations with confidence intervals” is now “Descriptive Statistics and Correlations”.

Tables in Quarto documents

This part is new rather than changed. apaTables 4.0 places tables directly in Quarto documents formatted by the apaquarto extension, which produces APA-style manuscripts as PDF, Word or HTML. Build the table on one line, and pass it to the function named for the document format on the next. In a .qmd document rendered with apaquarto, a table chunk looks like this:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-correlations
#| message: false
#| warning: true
library(apaTables)
my_table <- apa.cor.table(data = attitude)
apa.quarto.pdf(x = my_table)
```

The #| label: line must begin with tbl-; without it Quarto does not treat the chunk as a table.

For a full walkthrough, see the companion vignette:

vignette("apaquarto-usage", package = "apaTables")

Dependency changes

apaTables 4.0 needs R 4.1.0 or later (2.0.8 needed R 3.1.2). The boot, tibble and methods packages are no longer required. The flextable and officer packages are new requirements; they write the Word and HTML files. knitr, which 2.0.8 only suggested, is now required. MBESS is still required, as in 2.0.8.

If you used version 3.0.0 or 3.0.1 from GitHub

Those versions were never released to CRAN. In 3.0, apa.cor.table() had show.pvalue before landscape; in 4.0 it comes after, as the last argument, so a 3.0 call that gave both without names now needs them named. Those versions also had two functions that 4.0 removes. apa.knit.table.for.pdf() and apa.knit.table.for.papaja() wrote LaTeX through the kableExtra package. For a table in a PDF, place it in a Quarto document rendered with apaquarto:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-correlations
#| message: false
#| warning: true
library(apaTables)
my_table <- apa.cor.table(data = attitude)
apa.quarto.pdf(x = my_table)
```

For a Word file, use apa.save():

my_table <- apa.cor.table(data = attitude)
apa.save(filename = "Table1.docx", my_table)

The kableExtra and papaja packages are no longer listed among the apaTables dependencies.
